newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso woes not over yet-bankers.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso woes not over yet-bankers.

text.p: The Philippines could be forced into a drawn-out defence of its currency but was unlikely to succumb to the kind of speculative pressure that forced Thailand to float the baht, bankers said on Wednesday.
"I hope the speculators don't move to the Philippines and think the Philippines would have to bite the bullet as well," said Banco Santander treasurer Antonio Agcaoili.
"They're saying the local currency is likewise overvalued and therefore fundamentals don't support the peso-dollar level," he said.
Exporters have been urging the government to allow a weaker peso to make their products more competitive in the world market.
Thailand on Wednesday began a managed float of its currency, ending an exchange rate system that pegged the baht to a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.

The Philippine Central Bank put up a strong defence of the peso after the Thai currency announcement on Wednesday morning, raising its overnight borrowing rate by a total of nine percentage points to 24 percent and selling dollars heavily.
The peso closed at 26.376 from a previous 26.374. Speculation on the peso drove volume in the market to a record $1.05 billion.
Thailand's persistent financial woes have affected the Philippines with investors drawing comparisons with its economy and Thailand's, where an overheated property market has hurt the finance sector.
Nervous sentiment about the Philippine economy has hit Manila's stock market, which ended down 1.89 per cent on Wednesday at 2,764.89 points.
Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said the Philippines won't be forced into the same situation as Thailand.
"Thailand tended to peg its currency. Ours is managed but market-oriented," he said.
"I do not believe the Philippines will be forced to a change in exchange rate policy," said Hongkong and Shanghai Bank treasurer Mark Boyne, adding that Philippine economic fundamentals remain good.
But because of the spillover effect of the Thai policy change, he said the Central Bank's key overnight borrowing rate was not likely to fall below 15 percent for the rest of the month.

"I think the problem had been more drawn-out than initially expected and therefore rates would have to stay higher than people expected," he said. "I think the Central Bank will adopt a cautious policy."
Speculators, however, may be further discouraged from picking on the peso by the absence of offshore spot trading through which the Thai currency was assaulted, said Santander's Agcaoili.
"Speculators cannot really drive the peso down," Jaime Panganiban, treasurer at Bank of America, said.
He cited Bankers Association rules which impose a temporary halt in peso trading if it moves more than 1.5 percent from its opening rate.
Documentation requirements by the Central Bank also make it difficult to buy large amounts of dollars, he added.
Although slightly higher interest rates and a weaker peso may result from the recent developments, the impact would be short-lived, de Ocampo said.
"An IMF team is in town and they're about to leave here giving us a clean bill of health and a lot of strong statements that our economy is in good shape," he said.
-- Manila newsroom (63 2) 841-8937
